title: Adding and subtracting fractions
summary: Put fractions side by side on bars, then add and subtract them. When the denominators are different, make the parts the same size first.
guide: Each bar is one whole. The blue parts are already coloured: that is what you have. The parts you shade turn orange: that is what you add.
When the {{term:denominator}}s are the same, all the parts are the same size. So you just count parts: add the numerators and keep the denominator.

When the denominators are different, the parts are different sizes and you can't count them together. Use the + and − buttons to split the bar again until the parts are the same size. This is called finding a {{term:common-denominator}}.

same-sevenths.title: Sevenths and sevenths
same-sevenths.prompt: The bar has 7 equal parts and {{frac:2/7}} of it is already blue. First, predict: what is {{frac:2/7}} + {{frac:3/7}}? Then shade {{frac:3/7}} more and see if you were right.
same-sevenths.hint: {{frac:3/7}} means 3 of the 7 parts. Shade just 3 white parts; the blue parts stay where they are.
same-sevenths.success: Well done! 2 sevenths and 3 sevenths make 5 sevenths: {{frac:2/7}} + {{frac:3/7}} = {{frac:5/7}}
same-sevenths.why: Your friend says the answer is {{frac:5/14}}, because they added 2 and 3 and also added 7 and 7. Use the bar to explain why they are wrong.
same-sevenths.model: The denominator 7 tells you the size of each part: one seventh of the bar. When you add sevenths, the parts don't change size; there are just more of them. So you add the numerators (2 + 3 = 5) and the denominator stays 7. Also, {{frac:5/14}} is less than {{frac:1/2}}, but the bar shows the answer is more than half.

feedback.too-big: That's too much. The blue parts are already there; shade only {{frac:3/7}}, which is 3 more parts.
feedback.too-small: Not enough yet. You need to shade 3 white parts.

half-plus-quarter.title: A half and a quarter
half-plus-quarter.prompt: Half the bar is blue. We want to add {{frac:1/4}} of the bar. First, predict: what is {{frac:1/2}} + {{frac:1/4}}? But you can't shade a quarter on a bar with only 2 parts! Use + to make more parts until you can shade {{frac:1/4}}, then shade it.
half-plus-quarter.hint: Split the bar into 4 equal parts. The blue half is now 2 parts out of 4. Shade one more part.
half-plus-quarter.success: Great! A half is the same as {{frac:2/4}}, and {{frac:2/4}} + {{frac:1/4}} = {{frac:3/4}}
half-plus-quarter.why: Why did you have to split the bar into quarters before adding? If someone says the answer is {{frac:2/6}}, what would you tell them?
half-plus-quarter.model: Halves and quarters are parts of different sizes, so you can't count them together. When you split the bar into 4 equal parts, the half becomes 2 quarters. Now all the parts are the same size: 2 quarters and 1 quarter make 3 quarters. {{frac:2/6}} can't be right: {{frac:2/6}} is even less than {{frac:1/2}}, but we added something to a half.

feedback.too-big: That's too much. Add only {{frac:1/4}} of the bar. When the bar has 2 parts, each part is a half, not a quarter; use + to make more parts first.
feedback.too-small: Not enough yet. You need to add {{frac:1/4}} of the bar. How many parts does the bar need so that you can shade a quarter?

subtract-unlike.title: Three quarters take away a third
subtract-unlike.prompt: What is {{frac:3/4}} − {{frac:1/3}}? First, predict: is the answer more or less than a half? Then use + and − to split both bars again until their parts are the same size, and write the answer.
subtract-unlike.hint: Look for a number of parts that both 4 and 3 divide into. When both bars have the same number of parts, count the shaded parts and subtract.
subtract-unlike.success: That's right! You turned both fractions into twelfths: {{frac:9/12}} − {{frac:4/12}} = {{frac:5/12}}
subtract-unlike.why: Someone subtracted the numerators and the denominators (3 − 1 = 2 and 4 − 3 = 1) and wrote {{frac:2/1}}. Why can't that be right?
subtract-unlike.model: {{frac:2/1}} means 2 whole bars! But we took something away from {{frac:3/4}}, which is less than one whole, so the answer must be less than {{frac:3/4}}. The denominator tells you the size of the parts, and you can't subtract sizes like that. First turn both fractions into twelfths: {{frac:9/12}} and {{frac:4/12}}. Now the parts are the same size, and 9 twelfths take away 4 twelfths is 5 twelfths.

feedback.tops-and-bottoms: {{frac:2/1}} means 2 whole bars, but {{frac:3/4}} is less than one whole! Don't subtract the numerators and denominators separately. First split the bars so their parts are the same size.
feedback.too-big: Your answer is bigger than the right answer. Split both bars into the same number of parts and count the shaded parts.
feedback.too-small: Your answer is smaller than the right answer. Split both bars into the same number of parts and count the shaded parts.

mixed-sum.title: Adding a mixed number
mixed-sum.prompt: {{mixed:1 1/2}} is blue: one whole bar and half of the second bar. Add {{frac:3/4}} more. First, predict: will the answer be more than 2? Then write the answer as a {{term:mixed-number}}.
mixed-sum.hint: The bars have 4 parts. Shade 3 white parts. When the second bar is full, you have another whole. How many whole bars and how many quarters are shaded now?
mixed-sum.success: Well done! Two whole bars and a quarter of the third: {{mixed:1 1/2}} + {{frac:3/4}} = {{mixed:2 1/4}}
mixed-sum.why: Together, {{frac:1/2}} and {{frac:3/4}} came to more than one whole. Use the bars to explain why the whole-number part of your answer is 2, not 1.
mixed-sum.model: {{frac:1/2}} is the same as {{frac:2/4}}, and {{frac:2/4}} + {{frac:3/4}} = {{frac:5/4}}. Four of those 5 quarters make a whole bar, and 1 quarter is left over. So we made a new whole: the 1 we started with plus this new one makes 2, and {{frac:1/4}} is left: {{mixed:2 1/4}}.

feedback.not-mixed: That's the right amount! Now write it as a mixed number: how many whole bars are shaded, and what fraction of the next bar? The numerator must be smaller than the denominator.
feedback.tops-and-bottoms: Don't add the numerators and denominators separately. First change {{frac:1/2}} into quarters, then add.
feedback.too-small: Not enough. Remember, four quarters make one whole. Count the whole bars again.
feedback.too-big: Too much. Count the whole bars and the shaded quarters again.
